A machinery producer sources a critical precision component from a single supplier that holds unique tooling and process know-how; qualifying an alternative would take 18 months and significant engineering effort. The supplier has recently been acquired by a competitor's parent company, raised prices twice, and slipped on delivery dates. Redesigning the product to use a different component is possible but would delay the next product generation.

Formulate a supply risk strategy for the critical component. Weigh dual-sourcing, strategic inventory, contractual protections, partial vertical integration, and product redesign; recommend a portfolio of actions with timeline and cost logic, and define the triggers that would escalate from mitigation to full independence from the supplier.

# Supply Risk Strategy: Escaping a Hostage Position on a Single-Source Precision Component

## Framing: What This Situation Actually Is

Five observations, most of which get missed because procurement organizations classify this as a sourcing problem.

**1. This stopped being a supply problem the day the acquisition closed. It is now a competitive intelligence problem with a supply symptom.** Two price increases and slipped deliveries cost you money. The larger exposure is that a competitor's parent now sits inside your bill of materials with visibility into your volumes, your seasonality, your spec revisions, your engineering change requests, and — if you have been sharing roadmaps the way good partners do — your next-generation design intent. **Assume every drawing, forecast, and RFQ you have sent them in the last two quarters has been read by a competitor's product planning team.** That assumption costs nothing to adopt and changes your behavior today.

**2. The price increases and delivery slips may not be malice, and it does not matter.** They could equally be integration chaos, capacity reallocated to the parent's internal demand, or a departing account team. You cannot know intent, and you will never know it reliably. **Build a strategy that is robust to intent rather than dependent on diagnosing it.** The practical rule: negotiate as though the relationship continues, prepare as though it ends, and never let the two programs share a communication channel.

**3. "18 months to qualify an alternative" is a claim, not a physical constant.** Decomposed, that number is almost always a serial concatenation of steps that are only serial by habit, plus one genuine long pole. In precision components the long pole is usually tooling lead time or life-testing rig hours — both of which are purchasable. A parallelized program with tooling ordered at risk, additional test capacity bought outright, and a *staged* qualification scope typically lands at 9–12 months. That difference is the entire strategy.

**4. Dual-sourcing is not currently an available option, so stop debating it.** You cannot dual-source a part no second party can make yet. Qualification is the *precondition* for dual-sourcing, which means the real question is not "dual-source or not" but "what buys us survival during the qualification window." That window is the only thing that matters for the next four quarters.

**5. The second source does not need to be cost-competitive. It needs to exist.** The standard objection — "our volume can't support two suppliers" — misprices the asset. You are not buying units, you are buying an option on continued production. An alternate supplier running 5–10% of volume at a 25% price premium plus a capacity retainer is not a cost failure; it is an insurance policy costing perhaps $400–700K a year against an exposure of several million dollars *per month*. Price it as insurance and the argument ends.

**Illustrative parameters used throughout** (replace with actuals in week one): component cost ~$1,100/unit, ~9,000 units/year, ~$10M annual spend; the component gates ~$180M of machine revenue at ~40% contribution margin, i.e. **~$6M of contribution per month of production stoppage.**

---

## Phase 0: The 30-Day Diagnostic

Thirty days, not ninety. You are already bleeding, and the most valuable actions have lead times.

**1. Contract archaeology, week one.** Does the existing agreement contain a change-of-control clause, and did the acquisition trigger a right of renegotiation or termination? Who legally owns the tooling — and if you own it, do you have a documented right of access and removal, or only a line in a purchase order? Were the price increases mechanically permitted, or were they unilateral breaches you accepted by paying? **Is there an end-of-life / last-time-buy notice obligation, and how long is it?** That number sets the floor on your inventory sizing. Also check whether the merger was reviewed by any competition authority and whether continuity-of-supply or non-discrimination commitments were made as a condition of clearance.

**2. Requalification decomposition, engineering-owned.** Force the 18 months onto a page as discrete work packages with dependencies, and mark each as *hard-serial*, *parallelizable*, or *purchasable*:

| Work package | Serial baseline | Compressed | Compression lever |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supplier identification, NDA, capability audit | 2 mo | 3 wk | Run 4–6 candidates in parallel; pay for audits |
| Process development at candidate | 3–4 mo | 2–3 mo | Fund development, don't ask them to invest |
| Tooling design and build | 5–7 mo | 5–7 mo | **Hard long pole — order at risk in month 1** |
| First articles, dimensional/metallurgical validation | 2 mo | 1 mo | Pre-book metrology capacity |
| Process capability runs (Cpk) | 1–2 mo | 1 mo | Parallel across two candidates |
| Component accelerated life testing | 3–6 mo | 2–3 mo | **Buy more rigs; run 24/7** |
| System-level validation on the machine | 3–4 mo | 2 mo | Overlap with component testing at risk |
| Certification / regulatory (if applicable) | 2–6 mo | 2–6 mo | Start file preparation now, before parts exist |
| Field trial / pilot fleet | 6–12 mo | staged | Qualify for one model / one region first |
| **Total** | **18–24 mo** | **9–12 mo** | |

**3. Requirement re-derivation — the highest-yield analysis in the whole program.** Take the component drawing and ask, from the machine's function backward: which tolerances, materials, and surface specs does the *system* actually require, and which were written around what this supplier happened to be able to do? In single-source precision parts, a meaningful share of the "unique process know-how" is protecting a specification the product does not need — inherited from a design decision made a decade ago and never re-examined. **If a tolerance band can be widened by 30%, the pool of capable suppliers may triple and the 18 months may become 9.** This analysis costs two engineers and three weeks.

**4. Exposure and inventory-bridge model.** Contribution margin at risk per month of stoppage. Current on-hand and in-transit coverage in weeks. Supplier's stated lead time versus actual over 24 months. Then the central number: **how many months of inventory are required to bridge to a qualified alternate under each scenario** (immediate denial, gradual allocation squeeze, orderly transition).

**5. Sub-tier and capability map.** Where does the know-how physically live — in the tooling, in a specific machine tool or coating line, in a proprietary process recipe, or in four named process engineers? Who are *their* suppliers? Occasionally the genuinely scarce capability sits one tier down at a firm you can contract with directly, and the incumbent's moat is an assembly and inspection step you can replicate. Also map the reciprocal exposure: what does the competitor's parent buy from you, and which customers do you share?

---

## The Strategic Verdict

> **Buy time with inventory. Buy restraint with contract and information discipline. Buy optionality by qualifying an alternate at insurance scale, funded and started immediately. Buy independence by making the next generation architecturally indifferent to which supplier makes this part — and do not delay that generation to achieve it.**

The organizing principle, published to the program team:

> **We will not delay the next product generation to escape this supplier. We will make the next generation unable to be held hostage by anyone.**
